item.title: Functions
item.description:
What are we doing today

In this post we learn to write our own function. These are logic packaged into reusable and named blocks that lets us keep our code clean, readable and easy to fix (debug). Functions are one of the most important things in programming. And a good news, we have been using in-built functions already. Every time we’ve called print(), len(), or type(), we’ve been using a function.

What is a Function?

A function is a named block of code that does a specific task. You define it once, and call it by name whenever you need it — once, ten times, inside a loop, anywhere.

Without functions:

# Calculating a average for three different datasets
total1 = 22.1 + 19.8 + 25.3
average1 = total1 / 3

total2 = 30.5 + 28.1 + 33.2
average2 = total2 / 3

total3 = 15.0 + 18.4 + 20.1
average3 = total3 / 3

print (f"average1: {average1:.2f}, average2: {average2:.2f}, average3: {average3:.2f}")
average1: 22.40, average2: 30.60, average3: 17.83

With a function:

def calculate_average(numbers):
    total = sum(numbers)
    return total / len(numbers)

average1 = calculate_average([22.1, 19.8, 25.3])
average2 = calculate_average([30.5, 28.1, 33.2])
average3 = calculate_average([15.0, 18.4, 20.1])

print (f"average1: {average1:.2f}, average2: {average2:.2f}, average3: {average3:.2f}")
average1: 22.40, average2: 30.60, average3: 17.83

Same result. Less repetition. And if something needs fixing, you fix it in one place.

Anatomy of a Function

def greet(name):
    message = f"Hello, {name}!"
    return message
  • def — keyword that tells Python you’re defining a function
  • greet — the name you’re giving it (same naming rules as variables)
  • (name) — the parameter: a placeholder for the value you’ll pass in
  • return — sends a value back to whoever called the function

Calling it:

result = greet("Syeda")
print(result)       
Hello, Syeda!

The value you pass in ("Syeda") is called an argument. The placeholder inside the function (name) is the parameter. People use these words interchangeably — now you know both.

Functions Without Parameters

Not every function needs input:

def print_separator():
    print("-" * 40)

print_separator()
print("Some data here")
print_separator()
----------------------------------------
Some data here
----------------------------------------

Useful for things you repeat often — formatting, headers, dividers.

Functions Without Return

Not every function needs to return a value. Some just do something:

def describe_temperature(temp):
    if temp > 30:
        print(f"{temp}°C — Hot")
    elif temp > 20:
        print(f"{temp}°C — Warm")
    else:
        print(f"{temp}°C — Cool")

describe_temperature(35)
describe_temperature(22)
describe_temperature(10)
35°C — Hot
22°C — Warm
10°C — Cool

Good to know: If a function has no return statement, it returns None automatically. This is fine when you’re using a function purely for its side effects — printing, saving a file, updating something.

Multiple Parameters

Functions can take as many parameters as they need:

def calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_m):
    bmi = weight_kg / (height_m ** 2)
    return bmi

bmi = calculate_bmi(70, 1.75)
print(f"BMI: {bmi:.1f}")

Default Parameter Values

You can give parameters a default value, making them optional when calling the function:

def describe_reading(temp, unit="C"):
    print(f"Temperature: {temp}°{unit}")

describe_reading(22.5)          # uses default: °C
describe_reading(72.5, "F")     # overrides default: °F
Temperature: 22.5°C
Temperature: 72.5°F

Parameters with defaults must always come after parameters without defaults.

Returning Multiple Values

A function can return more than one value — Python packs them into a tuple automatically:

def analyse_readings(readings):
    average = sum(readings) / len(readings)
    maximum = max(readings)
    minimum = min(readings)
    return average, maximum, minimum

avg, high, low = analyse_readings([22.1, 35.8, 19.3, 38.1, 24.5])

print(f"Average: {avg:.1f}°C")
print(f"Highest: {high}°C")
print(f"Lowest:  {low}°C")
Average: 28.0°C
Highest: 38.1°C
Lowest:  19.3°C

The three variables on the left unpack the three returned values in order. This is called tuple unpacking and you’ll see it constantly.

Functions Calling Other Functions

Functions can call other functions — this is how you build up complexity in layers while keeping each piece simple:

def is_anomaly(temp, threshold=30):
    return temp > threshold

def classify_reading(temp):
    if temp is None:
        return "missing"
    elif is_anomaly(temp):
        return "anomaly"
    else:
        return "normal"

readings = [22.1, None, 35.8, 19.3, 38.1]

for temp in readings:
    status = classify_reading(temp)
    print(f"{temp} → {status}")
22.1 → normal
None → missing
35.8 → anomaly
19.3 → normal
38.1 → anomaly

classify_reading delegates part of its job to is_anomaly. Each function stays focused on one thing. This is good practice — functions that do one thing well are easier to understand, test and fix.

When functions start calling other functions, it would be good to skip the function definition and start from understanding the ‘main’ part of the code. And slowly trace back to see what the functions are doing.

Scope — Where Variables Live

Variables created inside a function only exist inside that function. They’re not visible outside:

def calculate_area(radius):
    pi = 3.14159          # this variable only exists inside this function
    area = pi * radius ** 2
    return area

print(calculate_area(5))
print(pi)                 # NameError — pi doesn't exist out here
78.53975
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[11], line 7
      3     area = pi * radius ** 2
      4     return area
      5 
      6 print(calculate_area(5))
----> 7 print(pi)                 # NameError — pi doesn't exist out here

NameError: name 'pi' is not defined

This is called scope. It means functions are self-contained — they don’t accidentally interfere with the rest of your code, and the rest of your code doesn’t interfere with them.

The rule: Variables defined inside a function are local to that function. Variables defined outside — at the top of your notebook — are global and can be read from anywhere, though modifying them from inside a function is something to be careful with.

Analogy: Imagine these local and global variables like your fave celebrities. Globally known celebrities are known by everyone, everyone can access their information everywhere very easily. But a not so popular new artist from Bangladesh will be known by very niche people in Bangladesh. Information is also not available.

Mini Examples to Try

These get progressively more involved. Each one uses concepts from earlier posts.

1. Celsius to Fahrenheit converter

def celsius_to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return (celsius * 9/5) + 32

print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(0))   
print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(100))
print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(22))  
32.0
212.0
71.6

2. Count anomalies in a list

def count_anomalies(readings, threshold=30):
    count = 0
    for temp in readings:
        if temp is not None and temp > threshold:
            count += 1
    return count

data = [22.1, 35.8, None, 38.1, 24.5, 19.3]
print(count_anomalies(data))         
print(count_anomalies(data, threshold=20))   
2
4

3. Clean a list of readings

def clean_readings(readings):
    # Remove None values and return only valid readings
    cleaned = []
    for temp in readings:
        if temp is not None:
            cleaned.append(temp)
    return cleaned

raw = [22.1, None, 35.8, None, 19.3]
clean = clean_readings(raw)
print(clean)   
[22.1, 35.8, 19.3]

4. Full pipeline — clean, analyse, summarise

def clean_readings(readings):
    return [t for t in readings if t is not None]

def summarise(readings, threshold=30):
    if len(readings) == 0:
        print("No valid readings.")
        return

    average = sum(readings) / len(readings)
    anomalies = [t for t in readings if t > threshold]

    print(f"Readings:  {len(readings)}")
    print(f"Average:   {average:.1f}°C")
    print(f"Anomalies: {len(anomalies)} readings above {threshold}°C")
    if anomalies:
        print(f"Highest:   {max(anomalies)}°C")

raw_data = [22.1, None, 35.8, None, 38.1, 19.3, 24.5, None, 41.0]

cleaned = clean_readings(raw_data)
summarise(cleaned)
Readings:  6
Average:   30.1°C
Anomalies: 3 readings above 30°C
Highest:   41.0°C

Notice clean_readings uses a different syntax inside the brackets — [t for t in readings if t is not None]. This is called a list comprehension — a compact way to build a list with a loop and condition in one line. We won’t go deep on it now, but it’s worth recognising when you see it.

Quick Reference

Concept Example Notes
Define a function def my_func(): Always followed by indented block
Parameter def f(x): Placeholder for input
Argument f(10) Actual value passed in
Return a value return x * 2 Sends value back to caller
Default parameter def f(x=5): Optional when calling
Multiple returns return a, b, c Unpacked as a, b, c = f()
No return function ends without return Returns None automatically

item.title: Conditions and Loops
item.description:
What are we doing today

So hopefully you have played around and can code! But is it slightly boring doing everything one line at a time. Right now, you cannot make any decisions or if you want to print each item in a list, you have to do it via indexing one by one. Not efficient!

In this post we give Python the ability to make decisions and repeat actions — two things that turn a few lines of code into something genuinely useful. These are the tools you’ll use in almost every piece of code you ever write.

If / Elif / Else — Making Decisions

A condition lets your code take different paths depending on whether something is true or false. This is the foundation of all logic in programming.

It works exactly like how we carry out logic in our minds. If it rains, I will take the umbrella, otherwise I won’t. That is the essence of the If-Elif-Else logic.

temperature = 35

if temperature > 30:
    print("It's hot outside")
It's hot outside

If the condition (temperature > 30) is True, the indented block runs. If it’s False, nothing happens.

Indentation matters in Python. The code inside an if block must be indented — 4 spaces or one Tab. Python uses indentation to know what belongs inside the block. Get it wrong and you’ll get an error. Try it!

Adding else

temperature = 22

if temperature > 30:
    print("It's hot outside")
else:
    print("It's not that hot")
It's not that hot

else is the fallback — it runs when the condition is False.

Adding elif — Multiple Conditions

elif stands for else if. It lets you check multiple conditions in sequence:

temperature = 18

if temperature > 30:
    print("Hot")
elif temperature > 20:
    print("Warm")
elif temperature > 10:
    print("Cool")
else:
    print("Cold")
Cool

Python checks each condition top to bottom and runs the first one that’s true, then skips the rest. Only one block ever runs.

Combining Conditions

You can combine conditions with and / or:

temperature = 28
humidity = 85

if temperature > 25 and humidity > 80:
    print("Hot and humid — not great")

if temperature > 35 or humidity > 90:
    print("Extreme conditions")
Hot and humid — not great
  • and — both conditions must be true
  • or — at least one must be true

For Loops — Repeating Over a Sequence

A for loop goes through a collection — a list, a range of numbers, anything iterable — and runs the same block of code for each item.

temperatures = [22.1, 19.8, 25.3, 18.0, 23.5]

for temp in temperatures:
    print(temp)
22.1
19.8
25.3
18.0
23.5

The variable temp takes on each value in the list one at a time. You choose the name — temp, t, value — it doesn’t matter as long as you use the same name inside the block.

Imagine you have a page with many shapes and you need to colour each one. It doesnt matter what colour you are using. You just need to color them. That’s what it means by the name doesn’t matter, what matters is whether you are being able to print it.

Using range()

When you want to repeat something a set number of times, range() generates a sequence of numbers for you:

for i in range(5):
    print(i)      
0
1
2
3
4

range(5) gives you 0 through 4 — five numbers, starting at 0. You can also control the start, stop and step:

for i in range(2, 10, 2):
    print(i)        
2
4
6
8

range(start, stop, step) — stop is always excluded.

Combining a Loop with a Condition

This is where things start to get interesting — and this pattern appears constantly in data work:

temperatures = [22.1, 35.8, 19.3, 38.1, 24.5]

for temp in temperatures:
    if temp > 30:
        print(f"{temp} is above threshold")
    else:
        print(f"{temp} is normal")
22.1 is normal
35.8 is above threshold
19.3 is normal
38.1 is above threshold
24.5 is normal

enumerate() — When You Need the Index Too

Sometimes you want both the item and its position:

temperatures = [22.1, 19.8, 25.3]

for index, temp in enumerate(temperatures):
    print(f"Day {index + 1}: {temp}°C")
Day 1: 22.1°C
Day 2: 19.8°C
Day 3: 25.3°C

enumerate() is worth knowing early — you’ll use it constantly when working with lists and later with dataframes.

While Loops — Repeating Until a Condition Is Met

A while loop keeps running as long as a condition is True. Unlike a for loop where you know how many times it will run, a while loop runs an unknown number of times — until something changes.

count = 0

while count < 5:
    print(f"Count is {count}")
    count += 1     
Count is 0
Count is 1
Count is 2
Count is 3
Count is 4

Infinite loops: If the condition never becomes False, the loop runs forever and freezes your notebook. Always make sure something inside the loop is changing the condition. If you do get stuck, click the Stop button (■) in the toolbar to interrupt the kernel.

While loops are less common in data science than for loops, but they’re useful when you’re waiting for something — a model to converge, a value to reach a threshold, a process to complete.

Break and Continue — Controlling Loop Behaviour

These two keywords give you finer control over what happens inside a loop.

break — Exit the Loop Early

Stop the loop entirely when a condition is met, even if there are items left:

temperatures = [22.1, 19.8, 35.8, 24.3, 38.1]

for temp in temperatures:
    if temp > 30:
        print(f"High value found: {temp} — stopping")
        break
    print(f"{temp} is normal")
22.1 is normal
19.8 is normal
High value found: 35.8 — stopping

Once break runs, the loop ends immediately. Everything after it in the list is ignored.

continue — Skip to the Next Item

Skip the rest of the current iteration and move straight to the next one:

temperatures = [22.1, None, 19.8, None, 25.3]

for temp in temperatures:
    if temp is None:
        continue        # skip missing values, keep going
    print(f"{temp}°C")
22.1°C
19.8°C
25.3°C

continue in data work: Missing or invalid values are extremely common in real datasets. The pattern of checking for bad data and skipping it before processing is something you’ll write constantly — and continue is often the cleanest way to do it.

Mini Project — Analysing 2 Weeks of Temperature Readings

Let’s put everything together. Imagine you’ve collected daily temperature readings for two weeks and want to do a basic analysis — flag anomalies, skip missing data, summarise what you found. Decide on your own rules. What are the values, what is an anomaly, what should the output look like.

# Two weeks of daily temperature readings (°C)
# None represents a missing reading — sensor failure, etc.
readings = [22.1, 19.8, 35.8, None, 23.5, 38.2, 21.0,
            None, 24.3, 20.1, 19.5, 41.0, 22.8, 36.5]

# Threshold above which we consider a reading anomalous
threshold = 30

# We'll collect valid readings and track anomalies
valid_readings = []
anomalies = []
missing_count = 0

# Loop through every reading
for index, temp in enumerate(readings):
    day = index + 1

    # Skip missing values
    if temp is None:
        print(f"Day {day}: No reading recorded")
        missing_count += 1
        continue

    # Flag anomalies
    if temp > threshold:
        print(f"Day {day}: {temp}°C — above threshold")
        anomalies.append(temp)
    else:
        print(f"Day {day}: {temp}°C — normal")

    # Collect all valid readings for summary
    valid_readings.append(temp)

# Summary
print("\n--- Summary ---")
print(f"Total days: {len(readings)}")
print(f"Missing readings: {missing_count}")
print(f"Valid readings: {len(valid_readings)}")
print(f"Anomalies detected: {len(anomalies)}")

# Only calculate average if we have valid data
if len(valid_readings) > 0:
    average = sum(valid_readings) / len(valid_readings)
    print(f"Average temperature: {average:.1f}°C")

if len(anomalies) > 0:
    print(f"Highest anomaly: {max(anomalies)}°C")
Day 1: 22.1°C — normal
Day 2: 19.8°C — normal
Day 3: 35.8°C — above threshold
Day 4: No reading recorded
Day 5: 23.5°C — normal
Day 6: 38.2°C — above threshold
Day 7: 21.0°C — normal
Day 8: No reading recorded
Day 9: 24.3°C — normal
Day 10: 20.1°C — normal
Day 11: 19.5°C — normal
Day 12: 41.0°C — above threshold
Day 13: 22.8°C — normal
Day 14: 36.5°C — above threshold

--- Summary ---
Total days: 14
Missing readings: 2
Valid readings: 12
Anomalies detected: 4
Average temperature: 27.1°C
Highest anomaly: 41.0°C

What this uses: - A for loop with enumerate() to go through every reading with its day number - continue to skip missing values cleanly - if / elif / else to categorise each reading - Two lists being built up as the loop runs — a pattern you’ll see constantly in data processing - A summary block using conditions to avoid errors on empty data

Notice the structure: The loop handles one reading at a time. The summary happens after the loop finishes. This separation — process row by row, summarise at the end — is exactly how data pipelines work, just at much larger scale.

Quick Reference

Concept Syntax When to use
if if x > 0: Run code when condition is true
elif elif x == 0: Check another condition if previous was false
else else: Fallback when all conditions are false
for for item in list: Repeat over a known collection
range() range(start, stop, step) Generate a sequence of numbers
enumerate() for i, val in enumerate(list): Loop with index and value
while while condition: Repeat until condition becomes false
break inside a loop Exit loop immediately
continue inside a loop Skip current iteration, keep going

What’s Next

You can now make decisions and repeat actions. The next piece is functions — a way to package logic you’ve written into something reusable, so you don’t repeat yourself across your code. That’s what we’re covering next.

item.title: Fundamentals of Python
item.description:
What are we doing today

Before we write loops, build functions, or touch a dataset — there are a handful of core concepts that everything else is built on. This post covers them all. Think of it as your reference page: read through it once, then come back whenever something in a later post feels unfamiliar.

Remember to follow along and play around

Variables — Giving Names to Things

A variable is a name that points to a value. Instead of writing the same number or piece of text over and over, you store it once and refer to it by name. > It is similar to calling a person by their name instead of referring to them by the description of their parents or ancestors

age = 25
city = "Berlin"
temperature = 36.6
age
25

That’s it. The = sign here doesn’t mean equal to — it means store this value under this name. You’re making a label, not solving an equation.

You can reassign a variable at any time:

age = 25
age = 26    # age is now 26, the old value is gone
age
26

Naming rules to know: - Names are case-sensitive — age and Age are two different variables - Use lowercase with underscores for readability: first_name, not FirstName or firstname - No spaces, no starting with a number, no special characters except _ > Learn a little more here

# Good names
user_age = 28
total_score = 150

# These will cause errors
2fast = 100       # starts with a number
my score = 99     # contains a space
  Cell In[5], line 6
    2fast = 100       # starts with a number
    ^
SyntaxError: invalid decimal literal

Data Types — What Kind of Value Is It?

Every value in Python has a type. Python figures this out automatically — you don’t declare it — but knowing what type you’re working with matters, especially when things don’t behave as expected. > You can think of this similar to peoples’ personality types (MBTI/Zodiac signs etc). You dont always need to know what personality a person is but knowing it helps you work better with them.

Integers — int

Whole numbers, positive or negative, no decimal point.

score = 42
temperature = -5
year = 2024

Floats — float

Numbers with a decimal point.

height = 1.82
pi = 3.14159
price = 9.99

Worth knowing: Even 10.0 is a float, not an integer — the decimal point is what matters, not whether the decimal part is zero.

Strings — str

Text. Anything inside quotes — single or double, both work.

name = "Alice"
greeting = 'Hello, Python!'

Strings can hold anything — letters, numbers, symbols — but they’re always text, not values you can do math with.

# This works
print(10 + 5)       

# This breaks
print("10" + 5)     # Error — can't add a string and a number
15
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[6], line 5
      1 # This works
      2 print(10 + 5)       # 15
      3 
      4 # This breaks
----> 5 print("10" + 5)     # Error — can't add a string and a number

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Booleans — bool

Only two possible values: True or False. Capitalisation matters.

is_student = True
has_gpu = False

Booleans might seem trivial now but they’re everywhere — every condition in a loop or an if-statement is producing a boolean behind the scenes.

Checking and Converting Types

type() — What type is this?

x = 42
print(type(x))      

y = "hello"
print(type(y))      
<class 'int'>
<class 'str'>

You’ll use type() constantly when debugging — especially when working with data that comes from files or the internet, where types aren’t always what you expect.

Converting Between Types

# String to integer
age = int("28")
print(type(age))   

# Integer to float
score = float(10)
print(score)       

# Number to string
label = str(42)
print(label) 
print(type(label))         
<class 'int'>
10.0
42
<class 'str'>

When does this matter? If you read data from a CSV file, numbers often arrive as strings. Trying to do math on them will break until you convert them. You’ll run into this the moment you start using pandas.

Operators

Arithmetic Operators

You’ve seen these already in the last post — a quick reference:

print(10 + 3)    
print(10 - 3)  
print(10 * 3)   
print(10 / 3)   
print(10 // 3)  
print(10 % 3) 
print(10 ** 2)  
13
7
30
3.3333333333333335
3
1
100

Comparison Operators

These return True or False. You’ll need these the moment you write your first loop or condition.

print(10 > 3)    
print(10 < 3)    
print(10 == 10)   # == checks equality and = assigns
print(10 != 5)    # not equal
print(10 >= 10)   
print(10 <= 9)    
True
False
True
True
True
False

Common mistake: Using = when you mean ==. A single = stores a value. A double == compares two values. Python will either throw an error or behave unexpectedly if you mix them up.

Lists — Ordered Collections

So far every variable holds one value. A list holds multiple values, in order, in a single variable.

temperatures = [22.1, 19.8, 25.3, 18.0, 23.5]
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
mixed = [42, "hello", True, 3.14]   # lists can hold different types

Indexing — Accessing Items

Lists are ordered and each item has a position — called an index — starting from 0.

names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]

print(names[0])    
print(names[1])   
print(names[-1])   #(negative index counts from the end)
Alice
Bob
Carol

Basic List Operations

scores = [85, 90, 78]

scores.append(95)       # add an item to the end
print(scores)           

print(len(scores))      # number of items in the list

print(scores[1:3])      # this is called slicing: items from index 1 up to (not including) 3
[85, 90, 78, 95]
4
[90, 78]

Slicing tip: [1:3] gives you index 1 and 2 — the end number is always excluded. This feels odd at first but becomes natural quickly.

Tuples — Like Lists, But Fixed

A tuple is similar to a list but immutable — once created, you can’t change it.

coordinates = (48.8566, 2.3522)   # latitude, longitude of Paris
print(coordinates[0])             
48.8566

You’ll mostly encounter tuples when functions return multiple values, or when working with data that shouldn’t change — like coordinates or RGB colour values. You don’t need to create them often, but you’ll see them, so now you know what they are.

Dictionaries — Key-Value Pairs

A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs. Instead of accessing items by position like a list, you access them by a meaningful name — the key. > Similar to how language dictionaries work. You want to look up a meaning, you find the wrod in the dictionary

person = {
    "name": "Alice",
    "age": 28,
    "city": "Berlin"
}

print(person["name"])   
print(person["age"])     
Alice
28

You can add or update entries:

person["job"] = "engineer"      # adds a new key
person["age"] = 29              # updates an existing key
print(person)
{'name': 'Alice', 'age': 29, 'city': 'Berlin', 'job': 'engineer'}

Why does this matter later? Dictionaries are everywhere in data work — JSON files (a common data format) are essentially dictionaries, and pandas works closely with dict-like structures. Getting comfortable with the key-value idea now pays off immediately.

Lists vs Arrays — What’s the Difference?

You’ll hear the word array a lot once we start working with numpy. It’s worth understanding how it differs from a list before we get there.

A Python list is flexible — it can hold different types, you can mix integers, strings, and booleans freely, and it’s great for general-purpose use.

A numpy array is built for numerical computation. It holds one type of data, is significantly faster at math operations, and supports operations across the entire array at once rather than item by item.

scores = [85, 90, 78]
scores * 2              # this just repeats the list, not multiplies each value

# With a numpy array, you can:
# scores * 2 would give [170, 180, 156], we will look further into this in the upcoming post
[85, 90, 78, 85, 90, 78]

Think of a list as a general-purpose container and a numpy array as a mathematical object. When you’re storing and organising things, use a list. When you’re doing computation across many numbers — which is almost everything in data science — you’ll want arrays. We’ll cover numpy properly in its own post.

Quick Reference

Concept Example Notes
Integer x = 10 Whole number
Float x = 10.0 Decimal number
String x = "hello" Always in quotes
Boolean x = True Capital T/F
List x = [1, 2, 3] Ordered, changeable, square brackets
Tuple x = (1, 2, 3) Ordered, fixed, round brackets
Dictionary x = {"a": 1} Key-value pairs, curly brackets
type() type(x) Check what type a value is
len() len(x) Count items in a list

Go here for further data types

What’s Next

With these building blocks in place, we can start doing something interesting — making code that reacts and repeats. So next Python starts making decisions and doing repetitive work so you don’t have to.

item.title: Set Up Your First Notebook
item.description:
What are we doing today

In the last post we talked about what Python is, the tools around it, and why we’ll be using uv for environment management. Now let’s get everything installed and actually run some code. By the end of this post you’ll have Python running, a notebook open in VS Code, and your first few lines of code executed. > The posts from here on are setup so that you follow along. I would suggest to also do any sort of playing you want. This is where we learn.

What so we need?

Here’s everything this post sets up, in order:

  1. Python — via uv, which installs and manages it for us
  2. uv — our environment and package manager
  3. VS Code — the editor we write and run code in
  4. Two VS Code extensions — so VS Code understands notebooks

Step 1 — Install VS Code

VS Code is the application you’ll write all your code in. It’s free, lightweight, and works well for everything from beginner notebooks to serious projects.

Download from: code.visualstudio.com

Click Download for Windows, run the installer, and keep all the default options. When it asks about adding VS Code to PATH — check that box. It’ll save you trouble later.

Step 2 — Install uv

uv is what we’ll use to install Python and manage packages. Open the Windows PowerShell — search for it in the Start menu — and paste this command:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Press Enter and let it finish. Once done, close PowerShell and open a new one. This is important — the new window picks up the changes the installer made.

Verify it worked by running:

uv --version

Note: You should see a version number printed. If you do, uv is installed

What just happened? That command downloaded and ran uv’s installer script directly from the internet. The new PowerShell window is needed because your system’s PATH — the list of places Windows looks for programs — only refreshes when a new terminal opens.

Step 3 — Install Python via uv

Now let’s use uv to install Python. Still in PowerShell, run:

uv python install 3.12

This downloads and installs Python 3.12 — a stable, widely supported version. uv handles the whole thing; no need to visit python.org or run a separate installer.

Check it worked:

uv run python --version

You should see Python 3.12.x printed.

Why uv and not python.org? Both work. But since we’re using uv to manage our projects anyway, letting it own the Python installation too keeps everything consistent and in one place.

Step 4 — Install VS Code Extensions

Open VS Code. On the left sidebar you’ll see a puzzle-piece icon — that’s the Extensions panel. Click it and search for these two, installing both:

  • Python — by Microsoft
  • Jupyter — by Microsoft

These extensions are what allow VS Code to run Python code and open notebook files. Without them, VS Code is just a text editor.

Step 5 — Create a Folder and Open Your First Notebook

Create a folder somewhere you’ll remember — your Desktop or Documents is fine. Call it something like python-blog or my-notebooks.

In VS Code: - Go to File → Open Folder and open that folder - Click the New File icon in the file explorer panel - Name it first_notebook.ipynb

The .ipynb extension is what tells VS Code this is a Jupyter notebook.

Step 6 — Select a Kernel

When the notebook opens, you’ll see a button in the top-right corner that says Select Kernel. Click it, then choose Python Environments, and select the Python 3.12 version that uv installed.

What is a kernel? It’s the engine that actually runs your code behind the scenes. When you click run on a cell, the kernel is what receives and executes it. Selecting the right one just means pointing your notebook at the Python installation you want to use.

A Note on Environments — Do You Need One Right Now?

In the previous post we talked about virtual environments — isolated Python setups that keep projects separate from each other. The honest answer is: not yet.

Right now you have one Python installation and no projects pulling in conflicting libraries. For the next several posts where we’re learning the basics, running directly from your uv-managed Python is perfectly fine.

Environments become important when: - You’re working on multiple projects that need different library versions - You start installing data science libraries like pandas or PyTorch - You want your setup to be reproducible — shareable with others or deployable somewhere

We’ll set up a proper environment when we reach that point, and we’ll walk through it in full when the time comes. For now, don’t let it be a blocker.

Let’s Write Some Code

You should now have your notebook open with a kernel selected. Click the + Code button to add a cell, and let’s go.

Cell 1 — Say Hello

# This is a comment — Python ignores anything after the # symbol
# Comments are how you leave notes in your code, for yourself or others
# It's a good habit to annotate what your code is doing

print("Hello, Python!")
Hello, Python!

Press Shift + Enter to run the cell. The output appears directly below it, and the cursor moves to the next cell automatically. That’s the core rhythm of working in notebooks — write in a cell, run it, see the result, move on.

Cell 2 — Basic Math

# Python can do arithmetic just like a calculator
print(10 + 3)   # Addition
print(10 - 3)   # Subtraction
print(10 * 3)   # Multiplication
print(10 / 3)   # Division
print(10 ** 2)  # Powers — this gives us 10 squared
print(10 % 3)   # Remainder — how much is left after dividing
13
7
30
3.3333333333333335
100
1

Run this cell the same way. Notice each print() gives its own line of output. The # comments on each line are there to remind you what each operator does — this is exactly the kind of annotation that makes notebooks readable when you come back to them later.

Tip: In a Jupyter notebook, you don’t always need print() to see a result. If the last line of a cell is an expression — like 10 + 3 — the notebook will automatically display its output. Try it: delete the print() and just write 10 + 3 in a cell. However, this only works for values — writing “Hello, Python!” alone will display it, but it won’t look or behave the same as print(), and plain text like Hello, Python! without quotes would just cause an error. For text output, print() is the reliable habit to keep.*

Cell 3 — A Peek at What’s Coming

# What if we want to reuse a value instead of typing it every time?
# We can give it a name — this is called a variable
# We won't go deep on this yet, but try running this and see what happens

result = 10 + 3
print(result)
13

You don’t need to fully understand this yet — we’ll break down variables properly in the next post. But notice that Python stored the result of 10 + 3 and printed it when you asked. That idea — giving names to values — is one of the most fundamental things in programming, and it’s what we’re covering next.

What You’ve Done

In this post you:

  • Installed uv and used it to install Python
  • Set up VS Code with the right extensions
  • Opened a real Jupyter notebook and selected a kernel
  • Ran your first cells and understood the Shift+Enter workflow
  • Learned what comments are and why they matter

👏 You are done with your first notebook!

item.title: Introduction to Python
item.description:
What is Python?

If you are here, you have probably heard about Python all around you but do not know where to start your journey. This is the right place. Begin with learning what it is, before learning how to do anything with it.

Python is a programming language — a way to give instructions to your computer in something closer to plain English. Unlike languages like C++ or Java, Python was designed to be readable and simple to write. That’s why it became the go-to language for so many fields you are probably aware about including data science and AI. Python has allowed programmers to focus more on where they are going with the code rather than focusing on writing the code itself.

Why is Python used extensively?

There are various programming languages - some which are used in nichely. However, Python is used extensively, especially as a default in data science and machine learning. Why so?

  • Python has a simple syntax allowing you to read and write the code almost like English sentences.
  • Python is an interpreter, so code can be executed as soon as its written.
  • It is free and open source. So you need no liscences or fees to be able to code.
  • It has various pre-built toolkits, so that you do not have to build everything from scratch.
  • It is versatile, meaning you can use it not only for your dataset exploration and graph building but also for building models as well as a user interface.

Libraries

The pre-built toolkits I mentioned earlier? These are the libraries. Libraries are the most important aspect of Python, that makes it easy to use for variety of tasks.

A library (also commonly called a package) is a collection of pre-written code that someone else built and very gratefully shared. Instead of writing hundreds of lines to load a spreadsheet, calculate statistics, or draw a chart — you import a library and call a function that does it in one line.

Think of it like the spices zou use to cook. You can gather everything and make spices from scratch at home but nobody does it because ‘packaged’ ones are convenient to use.

Here are some libraries you will hear very often:

  • numpy: core for scientific computing and handling arrays
  • pandas: expert at handling data structures like tables
  • matplotlib: handles your visualizations
  • pytorch: your support system for everything neural network

side note: There are in-built and external libraries too. All the ones mentioned above are popular external ones. Check out the python documentation for a in-depth search at https://docs.python.org/3/library/index.html or simply search about a library once you hear about it somewhere at https://pypi.org/

What is an IDE?

This is another term you will hear often once you enter the Python world.

IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment. It’s simply the app you use to write and run your code — think of it like Microsoft Word, but for programming. You can write your code there, edit, find errors, fix errors and run everything at the same place. It highlights your code, catches errors, and lets you run it all in one place. There are various IDEs available but we will be using VS Code throughout this blog. It’s the most widely used editor, especially in the data science community right now and is also a good start for beginners as it allows you to shift to other languages too.

Jupyter Notebook vs Python Script

Once you have an IDE, you’ll write Python in one of two formats. This distinction trips up a lot of beginners, so it’s worth clearing up early.

Python Script — .py

A plain text file (ending with .py) containing Python code. When you run it, the entire file executes top to bottom. This is what you use for finished work — automation scripts, production code, tools you want to hand to someone else.

Jupyter Notebook — .ipynb

A notebook where code lives in individual cells which you can run one at a time. Each cell shows its output directly below it. You can mix code cells with text cells — writing explanations, showing charts, and running code all in the same document. This is actually what is being used right now to write this blog.

You can think of pyscript as a finished cookbook that you wrote for distribution whereas the notebook is your personal messy notebook with your experimentation and outcome breakdown.

Environment & Dependency Management

Here’s where things get slightly confusing for beginners — and that’s okay, because even experienced developers find this part messy. When you install Python, you also need to manage:

  • Which version of Python you’re using
  • Which libraries you have installed
  • Keeping different projects separate so their libraries don’t conflict with each other

This is called environment management, and several tools exist to handle it. This is an essential part because it helps avoid conflicts — for example, one project might require PyTorch 2.x while another needs a different version.

Let’s walk through some of them.

Tool Function Category
Anaconda Manages Python, packages, environments Distribution & environment management
pip Install Python packages Package Management
venv Creates isolated python envrionments, uv is built on this concept Environment management
uv Manages Python versions, environments, packages, dependencies What we will be using mostly

side note: Find more: - anaconda - pip - venv - uv

Up Next

We will start with getting everything installed and set up, so you can start simple experiemnts yourself

This is the first post in my blog. Welcome!

This blog is a space to share my experiences, thoughts, and learnings in the field of programming, data science, and technology, as I continue my journey. This is more of a diary of my learnings and path, written as notes where I self talk (i.e. give myself instructions), so that I can refer back to them later. However, I do hope that my experiences will be helpful for other people too, especially beginners in this field.
